source: Lacosse, Duarte, Todd, McNamee (2026) Emerging Human-like Strategies for Semantic Memory Foraging in LLMs
finding: Llama-3 models doing the animal fluency task show cluster-then-switch structure like humans. They switch categories less often than humans, so they stay in a patch longer.
numbers: 699 human sequences vs LLM sequences from Llama-3 1B/3B/8B/70B (681 human and 2285 LLM kept after filtering, 35 items each). Mean switch ratio human 0.55, LLM 0.40 (Mann-Whitney p<0.0001). Spearman r=0.701 between human and LLM transition matrices (p<0.001).
limits: NeurIPS 2025 workshop paper, preliminary. Only animals. Llama-3 only. Each LLM sequence seeded with the first word of a human sequence.
agent_relevance: Without prompting, an LLM overstays in a category relative to humans. An agent loop cannot count on the model to leave a depleting line of attack by itself; code must fire the leave.

source: Lacosse et al. (2026) same paper: internal signals at the moment of a switch
finding: In Llama-3.3-70B the within-category token probability is high while staying and collapses at a switch. A linear probe can read switch events from activations, mostly with contrastive data.
numbers: Late layers (>39): non-switch within 0.0035 vs between 0.0005; switch within 0.0008 vs between 0.0007 (Mann-Whitney p<0.001). Probe on real human data AUROC 0.57 from activations vs 0.751 from output probabilities. Probe on contrastive pair data AUROC 0.96 neutral, 0.98 convergent, 0.97 divergent.
limits: Probe on natural data is near chance, so the high AUROCs come from exaggerated contrast sets. Single model for the activation work.
agent_relevance: The model's own depletion signal exists but is weak on natural data. Supports using an external yield counter (code) rather than the model's feeling of being stuck.

source: Leckie, Todd, Foster (2026) Signatures of semantic search in the activations of LLMs
finding: Patch depletion predicts leaving inside LLMs. The chance of switching category rises as the number of still-unsaid in-category items among the strongest internal concepts (J-space) falls. This is the MVT/Hills depletion logic found in activations.
numbers: Models: Gemma-2-9B, Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-7B. Switch probability vs in-category J-space supply: r>=0.31, p<0.0001 in middle layers for all models. J-space depletion beat depletion of the true category pool for all models except Qwen (F>=19.94, p<0.0001). Activations of the next category label rise before a switch.
limits: Small open models (2B to 9B). Only animal fluency. J-lens needs a precomputed lens; Llama-3B had none so they derived one. Qwen differs from the rest.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that depletion of the current patch is represented and drives switching in an LLM, so a yield-below-average trigger is not alien to the model. Still only on a recall task, not on solving problems.

source: Leckie et al. (2026) same paper: steering switch rate
finding: Adding a steering vector along a 'switch' direction raises or lowers how often the model leaves a category. Positive steering works better than negative.
numbers: Gemma-2-9B at layer 26: switch rate 0.29 baseline, 0.70 with positive steering, 0.07 with negative steering (Fisher exact p<0.0001 at best layers). Steering strength s=0.5 (0.1 for Qwen2.5-7B). Negative steering less effective for Llama-3.1-8B.
limits: Effect depends on model and layer. Needs white-box access. Authors note models are small compared with frontier models.
agent_relevance: The explore/exploit balance is a controllable dial in weights, but a closed-model agent can only set it through prompts and code triggers.

source: Heineman, Koenen, Varma (2024) Towards a path dependent account of category fluency
finding: Compared the foraging account (Hills 2012) with a random-walk account (Abbott 2015) by turning both into sequence generators and adding an LLM (Llama 2 Chat 7B) as a generator. An LLM alone does not leave the patch without an extra global cue.
numbers: Evaluation by n-gram overlap with a bank of human sequences. In words: the extra biases of the Hills model are needed for quality; the authors' category-transition addition improves it further; LLM-only generation needed a global cue to trigger switches. Exact scores were not extracted from the two-column text.
limits: Numeric scores not captured in this read. 7B model only. Does not settle foraging vs random walk.
agent_relevance: Even an LLM needs a separate trigger to leave a category, mirroring Hills' 'global cue'. Argues for a code-fired leave signal (S6) rather than leaving it to token-by-token generation.

source: Moore (2025) Optimal Foraging in Memory Retrieval: random walks and Metropolis-Hastings in modern semantic spaces
finding: Random walks on modern embedding spaces (e.g. OpenAI text-embedding-3-large) give MVT-consistent foraging. Metropolis-Hastings, the adaptive sampler, did not match human behaviour. The author says this supports Hills 2012 over Abbott 2015 in the sense of needing no complex acceptance rule.
numbers: Compared against human fluency data (a 141-participant set is cited). No headline effect size was extracted.
limits: Single short paper by one author. Embeddings only, not generative LLM behaviour. Numbers not captured.
agent_relevance: Suggests patchy structure is already in embedding space, so retrieval-based operator picking (O7 analogues) will cluster naturally; the MVT rule is about when to stop, not how to cluster.

source: Wispinski et al. (2023, TMLR) Adaptive patch foraging in deep reinforcement learning agents
finding: Deep RL agents (recurrent, trained on a 3D patch task with exponentially decaying patch reward) learn to leave patches like animals. They overstay the plain MVT optimum but match it once temporal discounting is included.
numbers: 12 agents (3 per discount rate, 4 rates). Overstay vs undiscounted MVT: +15.8 steps, SE 2.7 (p<0.05). Versus discounted MVT: +0.9 steps, SE 2.8, p=0.74 (not different). Higher discount rate gave behaviour closer to plain MVT. Patch reward r(n)=N0*exp(-lambda n), decay 0.01. Leaving time varied with patch distance as MVT predicts.
limits: Simulated environment with a colour cue giving the instantaneous rate, which makes the estimation easy. Only 12 agents.
agent_relevance: A learned agent leaves by comparing local rate with global rate, and the optimum depends on a discount: an agent with a hard budget should leave earlier than plain MVT says.

source: Wispinski et al. (2023) same paper: internal dynamics
finding: LSTM units of the trained agents show decision-variable ramping to a threshold, like monkey ACC recordings. Variability in leaving time came from ramp slope; the threshold-distance account was not significant.
numbers: Units with higher ramp slope for encounters with shorter leaving time (e.g. step 20: p<0.001). One component explained about 14% of LSTM variance.
limits: Threshold versus slope result not significant (Appendix A.1). Correlational.
agent_relevance: Supports the Kolling-style picture of an accumulating leave variable, so a code-side accumulator of 'evidence to leave' is a reasonable design.

source: Fonseca, Rios, Quijano, Giraldo (2025) World Models Unlock Optimal Foraging Strategies in RL Agents
finding: DreamerV2 (a world-model agent) leaves patches near the MVT step count. PPO (model-free) does not, and is much more variable. Agents tended to overstay, as animals do.
numbers: Four patch spacings (3, 5, 7, 9 spaces). Three training runs per algorithm. For DreamerV2 the MVT optimum fell within the interquartile range in all four scenarios and within +-1 quartile in at least three. For PPO the MVT value was outside the interquartile range in all four scenarios. R2D2 was compared on training score only.
limits: Small grid task; 3 training runs; no p-values reported. The 'anticipation' explanation is not isolated by an ablation.
agent_relevance: Planning ahead (a model of what the patch will yield) is what gets leave times right. A scaffold that makes the model predict the next step's yield before continuing may help S6 triggers more than a raw threshold.

source: Qian and Liu (2025) Scent of Knowledge: InForage, information foraging for search-enhanced reasoning
finding: Trains Qwen2.5 3B (and 7B) with RL to search iteratively. Reward = outcome + an information-gain term (max coverage of expected evidence), multiplied by an efficiency penalty that decays with every step past two. Beats Search-R1 and RAG baselines.
numbers: Reward R = gamma^max(0,T-2) * (R_outcome + alpha*R_gain). Two columns read cleanly: InForage 42.1 / 59.7 vs Search-R1-GRPO 40.9 / 55.2 vs Search-R1-PPO 32.3 / 53.7. Ablation: removing the efficiency penalty hurt, except on their own long-chain real-web dataset. PPO beat GRPO generally. 7B better than 3B.
limits: Table column labels were scrambled in text extraction; do not quote the pair as a named benchmark. Training method, not a prompt scaffold. The 'leave' rule is a learned step discount, not an MVT threshold.
agent_relevance: A working LLM-loop use of foraging ideas: pay for information gained, charge for steps. The step discount is the nearest thing to a rate-of-return cutoff; it helps on short tasks but not on tasks that truly need long chains.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) SCOUT: Active Information Foraging for Long-Text Understanding
finding: An agent explores a very long document and keeps a small evidence state. It stops when a gap-diagnosis step says the state is sufficient for the query. Matches or beats frontier long-context models at about a tenth of the tokens.
numbers: LOOGLE-V2 table (first score column): SCOUT 78.7 at 29.7k tokens vs Gemini-3-Pro 68.5 at 273.9k, GPT-5.1-chat 58.6 at 135.9k, Claude-Sonnet-4.5 42.5 at 100.9k, Claude Code 46.0 at 302.2k, MemAgent 31.6 at 408.1k. Token efficiency (acc/cost) 2.63 vs 0.25 for Gemini-3-Pro. On the BENCH table SCOUT 85.6 at 21.4k tokens, efficiency 4.01. Text claims over 8x token reduction versus Gemini-3-Pro.
limits: Which task each score column is was not confirmed from the extracted table. Stopping is by sufficiency of evidence, not by comparing yield rate to a long-run average, so it is information foraging, not MVT. Token cost is not in the reward.
agent_relevance: Stopping on 'enough evidence' is cheap and strong in practice. An MVT rule would add a second stop: quit when the last probes added little even if the state is not yet sufficient.

source: Jiang (2025) Workflow is All You Need: DeepNews, information foraging for long-form writing
finding: Uses information foraging theory to justify a retrieval step with a 10:1 ratio of retrieved material to output. Finds a 'knowledge cliff': below a retrieval amount, factual quality collapses.
numbers: Truthfulness collapses when retrieved context is under 15,000 characters; above 30,000 characters the hallucination-free rate stays above 85%. Blind submission test with a media outlet: 25% acceptance for DeepNews on DeepSeek-V3-0324 vs 0% for zero-shot GPT-5.
limits: Single author, one domain (financial reporting), one outlet, few submissions. Foraging is used as inspiration; no patch-leave rule is tested.
agent_relevance: Shows the failure the other way: leaving a source too early (too little retrieved) is costly. A leave rule needs a floor on minimum sampling before it can fire.

source: Ragavan and Alipour (2024) Revisiting Human Information Foraging: Adaptations for LLM-based Chatbots
finding: A thought experiment, no data. Argues that chat interfaces are not patchy, so classic information foraging (cost-value of following links) must be re-derived, and offers hypotheses.
numbers: No sample, no measured result. Nine pages.
limits: Hypotheses only.
agent_relevance: A warning: a chat loop has no natural patch boundary, so the scaffold must define one (operator attempt, source, or query) before a leave rule can be applied.

source: Azzopardi and Roegiest (2026) Information Farming: From Berry Picking to Berry Growing (CHIIR 2026)
finding: Perspective paper. Claims generative AI changes search from foraging in others' patches to cultivating one's own, so patch-based foraging may become less dominant.
numbers: No measured result in the parts read (abstract and front page).
limits: Perspective, not an experiment. I read only the first page.
agent_relevance: Weak direct use. Reminder that for an LLM agent the 'patch' can be self-generated (a thread of its own reasoning), which is where depletion is hardest to see.

source: Kilpatrick, Davidson, El Hady (2020) Normative theory of patch foraging decisions
finding: Bayesian derivation of optimal leave rules for depleting and non-depleting patches. Patch leaving is treated as inference about patch quality, not a fixed rate comparison.
numbers: Gives optimal residence time and decision rules, mostly in closed form; includes a hierarchical model that learns the environment's resource distribution. No empirical sample.
limits: Theory. Only the abstract page was read for this line.
agent_relevance: Gives the rule an LLM scaffold would need: leaving depends on uncertainty about the patch, so one failed attempt on a hard-to-estimate patch is weaker evidence than several.

source: Kilpatrick and El Hady (2026) Resource depletion accelerates rate learning but not composition learning in patch foraging
finding: Bayesian model. Depletion speeds learning of a patch's rate but not of how many patches are rich. Reward-maximising and information-seeking policies diverge: learning the mix needs departures, so a forager that wants to learn underharvests.
numbers: The best departure rule (count prey vs time the gaps) switches once patch richness varies by more than about a quarter. Reward-maximising policy collapses onto a stable orbit over high-yield patches when patches replenish.
limits: Simulation and theory only. Abstract and first page read.
agent_relevance: At S6, leaving early to learn which operators work has a cost. A scaffold should say whether it is exploiting or learning and not mix the two.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang, Slivkins (2024) Can Large Language Models Explore In-Context?
finding: GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama-2 in simple bandit tasks mostly fail to explore. Only GPT-4 with chain of thought and an externally summarised history (sufficient statistics) explored well.
numbers: T=500 rounds, N=20 replicates. With the basic prompt at zero temperature, over 60% of GPT-4 replicates chose the best arm only a handful of times and showed suffix failures (never choosing the best arm after some time), like Greedy and unlike UCB or Thompson sampling.
limits: Bandits, not patch leaving. Older models. Summarising the history for the model is the fix, which may be infeasible in complex settings.
agent_relevance: Bandit cousin of our trigger. Raw-history prompts fail; a code-computed summary statistic fixed it. That is the same design as S6: code computes yield versus average, the model does not.

source: Harris and Slivkins (2026, v4) Should You Use Your LLM to Explore or Exploit?
finding: Splits exploration and exploitation into separate tests. Reasoning models are best at exploitation; tool use (code interpreter) and in-context summarisation lift non-reasoning models. LLMs are still worse than simple linear regression, but help propose candidates in large semantic action spaces.
numbers: Models: GPT-5.2, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano, GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, Qwen-2.5, Gemma-3, Mistral-7B, DeepSeek-R1 distills. GPT-5-mini got perfect FracCorrect on the MAB exploit puzzle. GPT-4 and GPT-4o improved with the code interpreter; GPT-4 beat GPT-5.2 on one contextual bandit task with it.
limits: Contextual bandit tasks, not depleting patches. Exact tables not extracted; only figure-level statements read.
agent_relevance: Use the LLM to suggest candidate operators or probes (where it is good) and code to decide when to quit (where it is not).

source: Li et al. (2026) LLM-Foraging: LLMs for decentralized swarm robot foraging
finding: gpt-5-mini is called at three decision points of a swarm foraging controller, including a 'search starvation' point after a robot has searched without success for 60 s. It beats a genetic-algorithm-tuned controller in 33 of 36 configurations.
numbers: 36 configurations, 360 trials, 53,189 LLM calls, 3 fallbacks. Mean relative gain +70%; +142% on clustered layouts, +49% on powerlaw layouts, smaller on random layouts; where GA leads the gap is at most 7%. Mean latency 6.6 s per call; reasoning_effort=low; re-queried every 30 s after the 60 s trigger.
limits: Gazebo simulation, TurtleBot3, not a language task. The 60 s starvation trigger is a hand-set timer, not a learned rate comparison. Gain is largest when resources are patchy.
agent_relevance: A published LLM loop in which code fires a give-up event after a fixed dry spell and asks the model what to do next. Closest working analogue of S6.

source: Kolling, Behrens, Mars, Rushworth (2012) Neural mechanisms of foraging, Science (background, from memory)
finding: Human fMRI: dorsal ACC activity tracks the value of switching to the average environment, opposite to vmPFC tracking of the current option. Bridges foraging and choice between options.
numbers: Not re-read this session; no numbers recorded here.
limits: Record from memory only. Needs checking against the paper by the human-side agents.
agent_relevance: The founding study of the S6 trigger idea; the machine studies above test the same comparison in code or weights.

source: Charnov (1976) Optimal foraging, the marginal value theorem (background; rule statement confirmed in the text of Wispinski et al. 2023)
finding: Leave a patch when its current yield rate falls to the long-run average rate of the habitat including travel time.
numbers: Not opened. The rule statement was confirmed in Wispinski et al. 2023 (leave when patch reward rate drops below average reward rate).
limits: Assumes known, deterministic depletion; a 2025 bioRxiv paper (next line) disputes determinism.
agent_relevance: The rule behind the S6 trigger. Needs a cost for 'travel', here the cost of switching operator.

source: Stochastic choice drives variability in patch foraging decisions across species (bioRxiv 2025, search snippet only)
finding: Argues the MVT is deterministic, so identical contexts should give identical leave times, and tests a stochastic leave rule across species.
numbers: Only the search snippet was seen; no numbers.
limits: Not opened; seen in one web search result.
agent_relevance: Real leave times are noisy; a scaffold trigger should have a tolerance band, not a razor threshold.

source: Marshall et al. (2013) How do foragers decide when to leave a patch? Baboons (search snippet only)
finding: Competing leave models tested on chacma baboons: Bayesian updating won in the experiment, a patch-MVT model won under natural conditions.
numbers: Only the snippet was seen. No numbers.
limits: Not opened. A boundary condition: the winning rule depends on the setting.
agent_relevance: MVT is not always the best-fitting rule; Bayesian updating can win when depletion is uncertain.

source: Gap note: no LLM test of a patch-leaving paradigm with a depleting reward found
finding: An arXiv search for 'marginal value theorem' with 'language model' returned zero hits. 'patch foraging' returned 38 hits, none a language-model run of the Kolling or Constantino and Daw tasks.
numbers: arXiv listing pages, 1 Nov 2026: 38 results for 'patch foraging' (title list read); 16 for 'foraging LLM'. LLM work found is semantic fluency (2), information-foraging-inspired systems (3), robotics (1), bandits (3).
limits: Search limits: the web search quota ran out and the arXiv API, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs refused requests (429), so only arXiv listing pages were used. Papers outside arXiv or phrased differently may exist.
agent_relevance: The test 'does an LLM leave a depleting source at the MVT time' appears not to exist yet. Our own bench could run it and would be new.

source: Cross-study pattern: external computation of the yield statistic
finding: Results improve when code computes the key statistic and the model reads it: summarised bandit history (2403.15371), code interpreter (2502.00225), fixed starvation timer (2605.01461), sufficiency gap check (2605.04496).
numbers: Qualitative synthesis of c17, c18, c19, c11.
limits: My synthesis; the studies differ in task and model, and none tested an MVT rule head to head.
agent_relevance: Supports S6 being fired by code from a running yield average, with the model only choosing the next operator.

source: Cross-study pattern: LLMs overstay in a patch without a trigger
finding: Unprompted LLMs switch less than humans (0.40 vs 0.55), need a global cue to switch (2405.06714), and fail to explore in bandits with raw history (2403.15371). Deep RL agents overstay plain MVT by 15.8 steps (2210.08085).
numbers: Synthesis of c01, c05, c07, c17.
limits: Different tasks and model families. Humans and animals also overstay (noted in 2512.12548), so overstay alone is not a machine-specific flaw.
agent_relevance: Default failure to design against: staying too long on a depleting operator.

source: Cross-study pattern: leaving too early is also costly
finding: A knowledge cliff below 15,000 retrieved characters (2512.10121); the efficiency penalty hurt on long-chain tasks (2505.09316); the world-model agent anticipates richer later yield (2512.12548).
numbers: Synthesis of c12, c10, c09.
limits: Weak evidence individually; one-author and ablation-level results.
agent_relevance: Give the S6 trigger a minimum sampling floor and a task-difficulty adjustment so it does not abandon a hard-but-fruitful operator.

source: Cross-study pattern: nothing found that uses 'yield below average' as a trigger inside an LLM agent loop
finding: Nearest working cases are fixed timers (60 s dry spell), step discounts (gamma^(T-2)) and sufficiency checks, not a running average-rate comparison.
numbers: Synthesis of c10, c11, c19.
limits: Absence of evidence from limited search (see c24).
agent_relevance: The S6 rule 'leave when yield falls below the average' is untested for LLM loops, so it should ship flagged as a design bet, not an established finding.
